prompt: A customer searches the help centre for 'money back' and the article she needs says 'refund'. Why does an embedding search find it when a keyword search does not?

choices.text: It compares meanings, and training put the two phrasings close together
choices.why: Right. The vectors of texts that mean similar things point in similar directions, whatever words they use.

choices.text: It keeps a list of synonyms that includes refund
choices.why: No synonym list is involved. That is the hand-kept trick embeddings replace.

choices.text: It ignores the words and searches by category
choices.why: It never sees a category. The categories in the lesson's picture came out of the meaning of the titles.

choices.text: It reads every article to the customer's question with a language model, one at a time
choices.why: An embedding search compares stored vectors with the question's vector; no model reads the articles at query time.

prompt: A model returns 1536 numbers per text, each a float32. How many bytes does one vector take?
WordLlama gives 'the dog bit the man' and 'the man bit the dog' exactly the same vector. What kind of model behaves like that?

choices.text: A contextual model with too few layers
choices.why: Even few layers let pieces see their neighbours, so order would move the vector a little.

choices.text: A static one that averages fixed token vectors
choices.why: Right. The two sentences have the same tokens, and an average of the same vectors does not depend on their order.

choices.text: Any model whose vectors are normalised to length 1
choices.why: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 normalises too and scored the pair 0.9795, not 1.0. Normalising does not remove order.

choices.text: A multilingual model that has been asked about an English sentence
choices.why: Language support has nothing to do with order; the cause is how the vector is built from the tokens.

prompt: A team wants to flag customer messages that do NOT ask for a refund, using the similarity to 'I want a refund' with a threshold. Why will that fail?
hint: Lesson 1, what an embedding is not.

choices.text: The threshold has to be different for every customer
choices.why: The problem is not the customers: the vectors themselves put a negation close to the sentence it negates.

choices.text: Short messages always score higher than long ones
choices.why: Length is not what decides the score here; 'I do not want a refund' is longer and still scored 0.892.

choices.text: A negated sentence scores closer than a paraphrase, so no threshold separates them
choices.why: Right. Negation changes the assertion and keeps the subject, and the subject is what the embedding captures best.

choices.text: Similarity scores are only defined between texts of equal length
choices.why: Every text gives a vector of the same dimension, so any two can be compared.

prompt: Training a model on pairs of texts that belong together, pulling each pair close and pushing the rest of the batch away, is called ___ training.
Which of these statements about an embedding are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The same text through the same model always gives the same vector
choices.why: Yes. There is no randomness at inference, which is what lets a stored vector be reused.

choices.text: A vector of a customer's message should be treated as personal data
choices.why: Yes. Inversion research rebuilt short texts from their vectors.

choices.text: Two models of the same dimension produce comparable vectors
choices.why: The coordinates of one model have nothing to do with the other's; the dimension only lets the arithmetic run.

choices.text: Each coordinate measures one nameable property of the text
choices.why: Information is spread over all the coordinates; none of them means anything alone.

prompt: One colleague scores all-MiniLM-L6-v2 vectors with the full cosine formula, another with the plain dot product `D @ q`. How do their results compare?

choices.text: The dot product ranks long articles higher, so the lists differ
choices.why: That happens only when lengths differ. Every vector this model returns has length 1.

choices.text: The numbers and the order are the same
choices.why: Right. With both lengths equal to 1, dividing by them changes nothing, so the dot product is the cosine.

choices.text: The cosine is always larger, though the order matches
choices.why: Dividing by 1 × 1 leaves the dot product exactly as it was.

choices.text: The order is reversed, because one is a distance
choices.why: Neither is a distance: both are similarities, higher is closer.

prompt: pgvector's `<=>` returns 1 for two vectors. What is their cosine similarity, and what does that say about them?

choices.text: 1: they point the same way
choices.why: That would be a cosine distance of 0. `<=>` returns one minus the similarity.

choices.text: −1: they point in opposite directions
choices.why: Opposite arrows have a cosine distance of 2.

choices.text: 0, so they are perpendicular
choices.why: Right. Cosine distance is 1 − cosine similarity, so a distance of 1 is a similarity of 0: arrows at right angles.

choices.text: It cannot be known without the vectors' lengths
choices.why: Cosine distance already divides the lengths out; it depends on the angle alone.

prompt: An index was created with L2 distance and holds normalised vectors. Someone proposes rebuilding it with inner product to get better results. What will change in the ranking?

choices.text: Nothing: for unit vectors both measures give the same order
choices.why: Right. For length-1 vectors the squared distance is 2 − 2 × the dot product, so the orders match. The rebuild buys cheaper arithmetic, not better results.

choices.text: The best results improve, because inner product was what the model was trained for
choices.why: The model's training measure matters, but with normalised vectors the three measures rank identically.

choices.text: The ranking reverses, because inner product is a similarity
choices.why: The database handles the direction; best first stays best first.

choices.text: Long documents start winning
choices.why: Every vector has length 1, so no document is longer than another.

prompt: A pair of tickets scores 0.35 with one model, and another pair scores 0.55 with a different model. Which pair is more closely related?

choices.text: The second pair, since 0.55 is higher
choices.why: Each model's scores sit in their own band. A higher number from a different model is not a closer match.

choices.text: The first pair, since lower scores are rarer
choices.why: Rarity depends on each model's band, which the question does not give.

choices.text: Neither: both are below 0.6, so both are unrelated
choices.why: With all-MiniLM-L6-v2, only 6.0% of ticket pairs even reach 0.4. A fixed cut-off like 0.6 means nothing across models.

choices.text: No telling: compare each score with its own model's band
choices.why: Right. Scores are not comparable across models; place each against the distribution of its own model on the same kind of text.

prompt: Two unit-length vectors have a cosine similarity of 0.68. What is the square of the L2 distance between them?
Order these medians and means that `crowded.py` measured, from the lowest to the highest.
items: MiniLM's mean for pairs with the same label
trap: Random arrows sit lowest, around zero: real tickets share a subject, so even WordLlama's lower band sits above them.

prompt: Marginalia replaces all-MiniLM-L6-v2 with a different embedding model. What has to happen to `index.npy`?

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the new model also returns 384 numbers
choices.why: Equal dimensions do not make two models' vectors comparable.

choices.text: Only articles edited since the change need new vectors
choices.why: Every stored vector came from the old model, so none of them can be compared with a question from the new one.

choices.text: Every article is embedded again with the new model, and questions too
choices.why: Right. Questions and documents must come from the same model, so the whole index is rebuilt.

choices.text: The old vectors are normalised again to match the new model
choices.why: Normalising changes lengths, not which model the directions came from.

prompt: A team judges its new search by asking five colleagues to try it and say whether the results look good. What is missing?

choices.text: A larger group of colleagues
choices.why: More opinions after the fact still measure impressions, not whether the right document came back.

choices.text: Questions with their answers decided before the search runs
choices.why: Right. Relevance judgements let you count recall@1 and recall@3 and compare two versions on the same footing.

choices.text: A faster machine for the test
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with whether the results are right.

choices.text: Asking the colleagues to rate each result from 1 to 10
choices.why: Ratings given while looking at the results are still opinions formed after the fact, and they cannot be compared between versions.

prompt: A customer pastes the error code `E-4471` into the help search. It appears in exactly one article. Which search is more dependable for this query?

choices.text: The embedding search, because it understands what the code means
choices.why: A code has almost no meaning to place; in the lesson the embedding search left the article holding `4.90` at rank 11.

choices.text: Either, since both read the same articles
choices.why: They rank by different things, and on exact strings they differed sharply: 8 of 8 first against 3 of 8.

choices.text: The keyword search: a rare exact string gets a high idf
choices.why: Right. One article out of many contains it, so BM25 puts that article first and matches nothing else.

choices.text: Neither, until the code is translated into words
choices.why: BM25 needs no translation; it matches the string as it is.

prompt: With `k = 60` and equal weights, document A is first in the embedding list and missing from the keyword list; document B is first in the keyword list and missing from the embedding list. How do they finish after fusion?

choices.text: A wins, because the embedding search was the stronger one on the lesson's questions
choices.why: RRF knows nothing about which list is better; with equal weights a first place counts the same in either.

choices.text: B wins, because keyword matches are exact
choices.why: Exactness plays no part in the formula; only ranks and weights do.

choices.text: Both are dropped, because each is missing from one list
choices.why: A document missing from a list just gets nothing from it; it keeps what the other list gives.

choices.text: They tie, each scoring 1/61
choices.why: Right. Each gets 1/(60 + 1) from the one list it is in and nothing from the other.

prompt: The share of test questions for which a relevant document appears among the first k results is called ___ at k.
Which of these steps belong to the half of a search that runs ahead of time, once per article? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Embedding every article
choices.why: Yes. It is the slow step, and an unchanged article keeps its vector.

choices.text: Saving the vectors with their ids in the same order
choices.why: Yes. The matrix and the ids are written together when the index is built.

choices.text: Embedding the customer's question
choices.why: No. The question only exists when the customer types it.

choices.text: Sorting the scores and keeping the top k
choices.why: No. Scores exist only once a question has been compared with the stored vectors.

prompt: Marginalia's team sorts new tickets by hand every day. Which method lets today's sorted tickets improve tomorrow's predictions with no training run in between?

choices.text: k-nearest neighbours: each sorted ticket is one more stored vector
choices.why: Right. Learning is appending; tomorrow's comparison simply includes today's rows.

choices.text: Logistic regression, whose weights adjust themselves as tickets arrive
choices.why: Its weights only change when it is fitted again; new tickets mean a new training run.

choices.text: Zero-shot classification, which learns from the labels the team adds
choices.why: Zero-shot reads no labels at all; it compares tickets with written descriptions.

choices.text: Centroids, which keep yesterday's averages fixed whatever is added
choices.why: A centroid that never changes ignores the new tickets; including them means recomputing the average.

prompt: In the centroid method, what is each desk's centroid?

choices.text: The training ticket nearest the middle of all 100
choices.why: That would be one ticket for the whole set; a centroid is computed per desk, and it is an average, not a ticket.

choices.text: The desk's name, embedded as a single word
choices.why: That is the bare-names wording of zero-shot, which scored 39; the centroid comes from labelled tickets.

choices.text: The renormalised average of that desk's training vectors
choices.why: Right. One vector per desk, put back on length 1 so that dot products compare directions.

choices.text: The test ticket the classifier is least sure about
choices.why: Test tickets never go into a centroid; they are kept out to measure it.

prompt: Tomorrow Marginalia opens a sixth desk, for gift cards, and no ticket has been labelled for it yet. What is the quickest way to start sending tickets there?

choices.text: Retrain the logistic regression on the five existing desks
choices.why: A model trained on five desks can only answer with those five; it has never seen the sixth.

choices.text: Average yesterday's tickets to make a gift-card centroid
choices.why: Without labels there is no way to know which of yesterday's tickets were about gift cards.

choices.text: Raise k so that more neighbours get a vote
choices.why: No stored ticket carries the new label, so no vote can ever choose it.

choices.text: Add a sentence describing the desk to a zero-shot classifier
choices.why: Right. A new label in zero-shot is one more description; labelled examples can come later.

prompt: The refunds desk must not receive tickets that belong elsewhere, even if a few of its own go astray. Which of its numbers should the team watch?

choices.text: Its recall
choices.why: Recall is how many of the desk's own tickets reached it; that is the number for a desk that must miss nothing.

choices.text: Its precision
choices.why: Right. Precision is how many of the tickets sent to the desk belong there.

choices.text: The overall accuracy of the classifier
choices.why: One number for all desks hides where the mistakes go; the confusion matrix and per-desk numbers show it.

choices.text: Its support in the report
choices.why: Support is just how many test tickets the desk has, ten each here; it measures nothing about the classifier.

prompt: A test set has 40 tickets. How many percentage points of accuracy is a single ticket worth?
hint: Lesson 4: on 50 tickets, one was two points.

prompt: Match each method to how many of the 50 test tickets it sorted correctly with MiniLM's vectors and all 100 training tickets.
Why does a recommender built on a reader's average have to skip the books she has finished?

choices.text: The model gives a finished book a score of exactly zero
choices.why: The model knows nothing about who read what; finished books score high, not zero.

choices.text: Finished books are removed from the catalogue automatically
choices.why: Nothing removes them; they stay for every other reader, which is why the skip is per reader.

choices.text: Her vector is made from them, so they score highest
choices.why: Right. Caio's three finished books sat at the top of his own ranking until filters.py skipped them.

choices.text: They only appear when MMR is switched off
choices.why: They appear with or without MMR; mmr.py excluded them from its pool before choosing anything.

prompt: A reader's vector is the renormalised average of the two books she finished, which are about different things. Which unread books does it put first?

choices.text: Books fairly close to both of her books
choices.why: Right. The score against the average is the sum of the two scores, scaled; Wuthering Heights led Lia's list that way.

choices.text: Books very close to either one of her books, whatever their score against the other
choices.why: A book close to one and far from the other has a low sum; Sense and Sensibility missed Lia's list for that reason.

choices.text: Books in the genre of the book she finished most recently
choices.why: The average ignores order and genre; it only adds similarities.

choices.text: The books most other readers have finished
choices.why: That is the popularity fallback for a reader with no books, not what the average does.

prompt: A shop lists thirty editions of Pride and Prejudice with nearly identical blurbs, and an Austen fan's five recommendations are five editions of that one novel. Which change addresses it?

choices.text: Showing fifty recommendations instead of five
choices.why: The editions would still fill the top of the list; a longer list only hides the problem lower down.

choices.text: Writing the genre in front of every blurb before embedding
choices.why: That pulls books of one genre closer together, so the editions would stay just as close to each other.

choices.text: Renormalising the reader's average a second time
choices.why: A vector of length 1 renormalised is the same vector; nothing in the list changes.

choices.text: MMR with λ below 1, or a rule of one edition per title
choices.why: Right. The editions resemble each other, which is exactly what MMR penalises; a rule on the title field catches it directly.

prompt: For Marcos, who has finished nothing, the lesson showed the most finished books. Why is that list weak evidence in this shop?

choices.text: Popular books have no vectors, so they cannot be ranked
choices.why: Every book in the catalogue has a vector; popularity simply does not use it.

choices.text: It rests on a few counts: the top book was finished by 3
choices.why: Right. With twelve readers, popularity is a handful of counts; with thousands it becomes a sensible default.

choices.text: Popularity is computed from the blurbs, which are short
choices.why: Popularity counts who finished what and never reads a blurb.

choices.text: The counts change every time the model is run
choices.why: Counting finished books involves no model and gives the same answer every time.

prompt: With λ = 0.6, a book's similarity to the reader is 0.50 and its highest similarity to a book already picked is 0.70. What is its MMR value?
hint: Lesson 5: λ times the first, minus (1 − λ) times the second.

prompt: Order one round of MMR as mmr.py runs it, and what follows.
items: Score each remaining book's similarity to the reader
Subtract the penalty for its highest similarity to a book already picked
Pick the book with the highest value
Move it from the pool to the list
Repeat until the list holds five
trap: The penalty is computed before the pick, against the books already on the list, never against the whole pool.

prompt: Why does anomaly detection with embeddings score messages by their distance from normal data instead of training a label for the odd ones?

choices.text: The odd messages share nothing, and new kinds keep arriving
choices.why: Right. Spam, foreign languages and noise are not one category, so there is nothing stable to learn a label from.

choices.text: Distances are cheaper to compute than a classifier's prediction
choices.why: Cost is not the reason. Lesson 4's classifiers were cheap too; they simply cannot answer none of these.

choices.text: A classifier refuses messages it has never seen
choices.why: The opposite: lesson 6's classifier gave every odd message one of its five labels.

choices.text: Normal messages cannot be labelled
choices.why: They were labelled: the 150 tickets carry one of five labels each. The odd ones are what cannot be described.

prompt: A shop's normal messages fall into five distinct topics. Which score is more likely to separate odd messages well, and why?

choices.text: Distance to the mean of all messages, because it uses every one of them
choices.why: The mean sits between the five topics, where no real message lives; that is how the spam hid at 16th in lesson 6.

choices.text: The k-th nearest normal message, since each topic keeps its own near neighbours
choices.why: Right. A normal message has a close neighbour in its own topic wherever that topic sits; an odd one has none.

choices.text: The distance to the longest normal message
choices.why: Length plays no part: the vectors all have length 1. Nothing in the lesson scores against one chosen message.

choices.text: The share of normal messages within 0.5, because a fixed radius is objective
choices.why: A fixed radius is a number picked by hand, and scores bunch differently per model, as lesson 2 showed.

prompt: Ana sets the cut-off at the 99th percentile of held-out normal scores instead of the 90th. What does she trade?

choices.text: Fewer false alarms, at the risk of letting more odd messages through
choices.why: Right. With k=5 in lesson 6, the 99th percentile flagged nothing by mistake and missed two odd messages.

choices.text: More false alarms, for catching every odd message
choices.why: That is the 90th percentile's side of the trade: three normal messages flagged, every odd one caught.

choices.text: Nothing, because a percentile of normal data says nothing about the cut-off's effect
choices.why: It moves the line, and the line decides both how many normal messages and how many odd ones are flagged.

choices.text: A slower detector, because a higher percentile compares more messages
choices.why: Every message is scored the same way whatever the line. Only the decision after the score changes.

prompt: A detector flags 10 messages, 6 of which are really odd, and there were 8 odd messages in all. What is its recall, as a fraction with two decimals?
A new product launches and many customers ask about it. The per-message flags barely rise, but most of the new messages have their nearest neighbour among each other. What is the right reading?

choices.text: A spam campaign, since similar messages arrived together
choices.why: Similar messages arriving together is what a new topic looks like too. Read them: in lesson 6 they were customers asking about a subscription.

choices.text: The detector is broken and should be rebuilt from scratch
choices.why: It is working: it describes the old normal faithfully. What moved is the traffic, not the detector.

choices.text: A new topic: drift to handle by adding a category and re-baselining with reviewed messages
choices.why: Right. It is not an anomaly in any message; the reference needs to learn the new normal, from messages somebody has read.

choices.text: Nothing, because only flagged messages matter
choices.why: The batch numbers are exactly what reveal a topic that per-message flags undercount.

prompt: Which of these can a detector that measures distance from normal messages, with an English-only embedding model, be expected to flag? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A message that is only random keyboard characters
choices.why: Yes. Noise has no near neighbour among real tickets; lesson 6's keyboard line ranked among the odd ones.

choices.text: A job application sent to the support address
choices.why: Yes. Its subject is far from every ticket, as m37 showed.

choices.text: A refund request for an amount far above the order's price
choices.why: No. By subject it is an ordinary refund request; the vector does not weigh amounts.

choices.text: An ordinary delivery question written in good English
choices.why: No. That is exactly what the reference is made of.

prompt: An embeddings response holds three vectors. Which field ties each vector to the text it came from?

choices.text: `index`
choices.why: Right. It is the position of the text in the `input` list; sort or look up by it rather than trusting the order.

choices.text: `usage`, which lists the tokens of each text
choices.why: `usage` holds totals for the whole request, not one entry per text.

choices.text: `model`, repeated on every vector
choices.why: `model` appears once, for the whole response, and names the model, not the text.

choices.text: `object`, which carries the text itself
choices.why: `object` just says embedding. The text is never sent back.

prompt: Ana calls the embeddings endpoint with plain `requests` instead of the SDK and gets a JSON list of decimal numbers. What would shrink the response, and what does she then have to do?

choices.text: Send fewer texts per request; nothing else changes
choices.why: That shrinks each response by shrinking the work, not the encoding. The same vectors still travel as long decimal text.

choices.text: Ask for `dimensions=1`, since one number is always enough
choices.why: One coordinate is not a usable vector, and lab-minilm refuses the parameter anyway.

choices.text: Compress the input text before sending it
choices.why: The input is small; the size is in the vectors coming back.

choices.text: Ask for `encoding_format="base64"`, then decode it as little-endian float32
choices.why: Right. That is what the SDK does on its own; lesson 7 measured 8,594 bytes against 2,203 for one vector.

prompt: A batch of 1,000 product descriptions is refused with 400, and one description in it is an empty string. What is the right fix?

choices.text: Retry the same request until the server accepts it
choices.why: A 400 says the request is wrong; it fails the same way every time, which is why the SDK does not retry it.

choices.text: Remove empty texts before building each batch
choices.why: Right. One empty string makes the server refuse the whole request, not just that slot.

choices.text: Split the batch into requests of one text each
choices.why: The batch is well under the 2,048-input limit. Splitting only multiplies requests; the empty one still fails.

choices.text: Switch to a model that accepts the `dimensions` parameter
choices.why: The refusal is about the input, not the output size.

prompt: A team truncates stored 1,536-number vectors to 512 by keeping the first 512 numbers, and compares queries truncated the same way by dot product. Search gets noticeably worse than asking the API for `dimensions=512`. What did they most likely skip?

choices.text: Converting the vectors to float64 first
choices.why: Precision is not the issue; float32 was fine at every size in lesson 7.

choices.text: Re-embedding the documents with the same model
choices.why: The prefix of a vector from a model trained for it is usable without re-embedding; the API does the same cut.

choices.text: Choosing a different tokeniser for the queries
choices.why: Queries and documents went through the same model; tokenisers decide tokens, not this ranking.

choices.text: Renormalising each cut vector to length 1
choices.why: Right. Cut vectors keep different shares of their length, so longer ones win for being long; lesson 7's renormalised cut matched the API exactly.

prompt: At LiteLLM's sheet price of $0.130 per million tokens for text-embedding-3-large, what does it cost to embed 4 million chunks of 250 tokens each, in US dollars?
With the client's defaults, a provider answers a call's first two requests with 429 and the third with 200. What does the calling code observe?

choices.text: A RateLimitError, which it must catch and retry itself
choices.why: The SDK retries 429 up to max_retries before raising; here the third attempt succeeded.

choices.text: The vector, returned normally after a short delay
choices.why: Right. In lesson 7 the call returned after 2.2 s and the program never saw the refusals; only the server log did.

choices.text: Two warnings printed, then the vector
choices.why: The SDK printed nothing; the refusals showed up only in the server's log.

choices.text: An empty response, since the first request failed
choices.why: The response carried all 384 numbers from the successful attempt.

prompt: A team moves its embedding code to the cohere SDK and calls `co.embed(model=..., texts=...)` exactly as before, with nothing else. What happens?

choices.text: Cohere fills in `search_document` and embeds the texts
choices.why: There is no default: the models from version 3 on require the parameter, and the SDK enforces it.

choices.text: Python raises a TypeError before any request is sent
choices.why: Right. `input_type` is a required keyword argument of the SDK's `embed`.

choices.text: The server answers with a 400 naming the missing field
choices.why: That is what a hand-written HTTP request gets. Through the SDK, the call never leaves Python.

choices.text: It works, because `input_type` only changes what the call is billed
choices.why: The input type says what the text is for; it has nothing to do with the bill.

prompt: An index stores Cohere `ubinary` vectors. Which comparison ranks them correctly against a query encoded the same way?

choices.text: A dot product of the packed bytes, read as ordinary numbers
choices.why: Each byte packs eight unrelated coordinates; multiplying bytes as numbers mixes them into a meaningless score.

choices.text: Cosine similarity after turning each byte into a float
choices.why: Same problem: the byte is eight bits, not one value, so its float means nothing.

choices.text: The count of bits that differ, fewer meaning closer
choices.why: Yes, the Hamming distance; quantised.py negated it so that higher meant closer.

choices.text: Euclidean distance between the byte values
choices.why: Distances between packed bytes measure the packing, not the coordinates.

prompt: `gemini.py` asked `lab-wordllama` for 128 numbers and their lengths printed as 1.0. Why can you not rely on that against gemini-embedding-001 at 768?

choices.text: labembed rescales cut vectors; Google says it does not
choices.why: Right. The lab's behaviour hid the step; the last part of gemini.py exists for Google's.

choices.text: Every embedding API returns unit vectors, so you can
choices.why: Google documents the opposite for its truncated sizes, and some models return vectors of any length.

choices.text: The SDK normalises every response it receives
choices.why: The SDK passes the values through; the lab server did the normalising.

choices.text: WordLlama's first 128 coordinates happen to have length 1
choices.why: A prefix of a unit vector is shorter than 1. The server divided by the length after cutting.

prompt: Why does Cohere ask what each text is for?

choices.text: To pick the price tier for the call
choices.why: The bill counts tokens; the input type does not change it.

choices.text: To detect which language the text is in
choices.why: Language has nothing to do with the input type; it names the text's role.

choices.text: To place questions near answers
choices.why: Yes. Search is asymmetric, and the model is told which side each text is on.

choices.text: To decide how many numbers the vector will have
choices.why: That is `output_dimension`, a separate parameter.

prompt: Marginalia keeps one million lab-minilm vectors in their `ubinary` form. How many megabytes is that, counting a megabyte as 1,000,000 bytes and nothing but the vectors?
Which of these did labembed accept and then ignore in this lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Gemini's `task_type`
choices.why: Yes. tasks.py got identical vectors for four task types, and the log recorded all four.

choices.text: Cohere's `input_type`
choices.why: Yes. search.py found 19 and 22 whichever type the questions were sent with.

choices.text: `output_dimensionality` sent for `lab-wordllama`
choices.why: It was honoured: the vectors came back with 128 numbers.

choices.text: A provider's model name such as `gemini-embedding-001`
choices.why: It was refused with a 404, not ignored.

choices.text: Cohere's limit of 96 texts per call

prompt: The same 20,000 vectors of 384 dimensions took 1536.0 bytes a vector in a `.npy` file and 1,676 bytes a row in a pgvector table. Where does the difference come from?

choices.text: pgvector stores each number as float64
choices.why: That would double the vector to over 3,000 bytes. pgvector stores four-byte floats, plus a small header.

choices.text: Headers, and pages that take whole rows only
choices.why: Right. The vector gets a header, the row gets one and a pointer, and the space left at the end of each 8 KB page is wasted.

choices.text: The primary key index is counted inside each row
choices.why: The primary key was the separate indexes column, 466,944 bytes for the whole table.

choices.text: PostgreSQL keeps the text of each vector beside it
choices.why: The table held only an id and the vector; there was no text to keep.

prompt: A team will keep 1,000,000 vectors of 768 dimensions in pgvector with one HNSW index. Which estimate of the disk they need is the right shape?

choices.text: About 3 GB, the raw float32 numbers
choices.why: That counts the numbers once. The table holds them with row overhead and the HNSW index holds its own copy.

choices.text: A little over 3 GB, since an index adds only links
choices.why: That is true of hnswlib's file, which stores the vectors once. pgvector's index stores every vector again.

choices.text: More than twice the raw numbers: table and index each hold a copy
choices.why: Right. In the lesson the HNSW index alone was larger per row than the table at 384 dimensions.

choices.text: Less than the raw numbers, since PostgreSQL compresses large values
choices.why: pgvector 0.6.0 declares its type STORAGE external: moved out of the row and never compressed.

prompt: Marginalia archives 60% of its help-centre chunks in one afternoon and deletes their rows from a pgvector table with an HNSW index. What gets the index back to the size of what is left?

choices.text: A REINDEX of the table
choices.why: Right. Rebuilding from the remaining rows is what halved the indexes in the lesson; CONCURRENTLY keeps searches running while it works.

choices.text: A plain VACUUM, which returns the freed space
choices.why: VACUUM took over two minutes in the lesson and changed no size: it keeps the freed space inside the files for reuse.

choices.text: Nothing, because DELETE removes the entries from the index at once
choices.why: After the DELETE every size stayed exactly as before; the rows are only marked dead.

choices.text: Raising hnsw.ef_search so the graph skips the deleted rows
choices.why: ef_search changes how much of the graph a query explores. It writes nothing and frees nothing.

prompt: A team needs its vectors to take about a quarter of their float32 size and wants each text's nearest neighbours to change as little as possible. Going by the lesson's measurements, what should it try first?

choices.text: Keep only the first quarter of the dimensions
choices.why: WordLlama cut to 64 of its 256 dimensions kept 0.642 of the neighbours: fewer numbers cost far more than fewer bits.

choices.text: int8
choices.why: Right. A quarter of the bytes plus one scale per vector, and 0.995 of the neighbours kept for both models.

choices.text: Binary codes, one bit per number
choices.why: That is a thirty-second of the size, not a quarter, and it kept only 0.705 and 0.600 of the neighbours.

choices.text: float16 applied twice
choices.why: There is no such step: float16 is a fixed two-byte format, which halves the size once.
